extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology/literary criticism (graduate-level readers analyzing narrative temporality, e.g., Proust)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical framework for describing and classifying temporal order in narrative (anachronies, analepses/prolepses), their types, functions, and relations to the 'first narrative'—with examples chiefly from Proust and classical texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal analysis limited to order
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict temporal analysis here solely to questions of order (sequence of events) and set aside questions of speed (duration), frequency, and mood/voice, which affect anachronies but are treated separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing anachronies focus on where in the story timeline the inserted segment lies relative to the 'first narrative' (order). Do not conflate this with duration/speed (chapter on duration) or narrative mood/voice (chapter on voice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachrony (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disruption of chronological order in narrative: any movement into the past or future with respect to the narrative's present (includes both analepses and prolepses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify narrative deviations from the story's present as anachronies and then analyze their type (analepsis vs prolepsis), reach, and extent. Examples: analepses in Proust, proleptic anticipations in other narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachrony's reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The temporal distance between the anachrony's locus and the 'present' moment of the first narrative (how far into past or future it reaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reach separately from extent: e.g., Ulysses' wound analepsis has a reach of several decades though its extent covers a few days. Use reach to compare relative remoteness of anachronies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachrony's extent
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration (how much story-time) covered by the anachrony itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record how long the detour covers in story-time (days, years, iterative series). Distinguish extent from reach because a long reach can have a short extent and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: External analepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: An analepsis whose entire extent lies before (earlier than) the beginning of the first narrative; it is external to the first narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External analepses function to supply 'antecedents' or background without interfering with the first narrative's prerogative (e.g., Un amour de Swann in the Recherche). Treat them as informative backfilling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal analepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: An analepsis whose temporal field falls within the temporal field of the first narrative (later than the first narrative's start); because it is internal, it risks redundancy or collision with the first narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze internal analepses for potential interference with the ongoing narrative; further sub-classify to determine function (completing vs repeating). Examples: Emma's years in the convent within Madame Bovary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed analepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: An analepsis whose reach goes back to a point earlier than the start of the first narrative but whose extent continues to a time later than the beginning of the first narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mixed cases as having both external and internal aspects (example: Des Grieux in Manon Lescaut). Consider both filling antecedents and interacting with the first narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterodiegetic analepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal analepsis that deals with a different diegetic line or storyline than that of the first narrative (a different character's antecedents or side-story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heterodiegetic internal analepses classically inform about another character's past (e.g., chapters giving a newcomer's antecedents) and generally do not disturb the first narrative's continuity; treat as explanatory backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homodiegetic internal analepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal analepsis that deals with the same line of action as the first narrative (same protagonist/storyline); because of containment, it poses a risk of redundancy or collision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate homodiegetic internal analepses into completing vs repeating types; examine how they fill gaps or re-present earlier material and how they alter reader understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing analepses (returns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal homodiegetic analepses that 'fill in' earlier gaps in the narrative—either temporal ellipses (omitted time intervals) or lateral omissions of situation elements—and so complete the first narrative retroactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the type of gap being filled: temporal ellipsis (missing time span, e.g., Paris 1914 recounted later) or paralipsis (omission of an element/person later supplied). Use these fills to reconstruct implied chronology (examples from Proust: Swann's death, Lady in pink revelations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralipsis (lateral ellipsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: An omission not of a time-span but of a constituent element of a situation that the narrative otherwise covers (e.g., systematically concealing a family member), producing a lateral gap later subject to retrospective filling-in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat paralipsis as omission of an element (character/event) rather than of a period; look for later analeptic disclosures that explain or reveal the omitted element (example: the 'girl-cousin' episode omitted from Combray narrative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative analepses / iterative ellipses
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospections that localize an event not to a single instance but to a class or series (e.g., 'a winter' or a repeated set of dinners); the analepsis refers to a repetitive or generic series rather than a uniquely dated moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize iterative analepses at the level of species/class; recognize when a single narrated episode functions as stand-in for many similar occurrences (e.g., the dinner at Rivebelle standing for prior dinners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeating analepses (recalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal homodiegetic analepses that retrace the narrative's own path—retroceptions or 'recalls' that allude back to previous narrative moments, often in short, precise allusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recalls are typically small, deliberate allusions (e.g., involuntary-memory reminiscences) that put past and present in comparison (analogy or contrast) and can retroactively change a past episode's significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred/postponed significance (enigma mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of anachrony to postpone important information or interpretation, producing an enigma whose solution arrives later and thereby reorganizes the reader's understanding of earlier events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize delayed revelations (e.g., identity of the Lady in pink, later explanations that change the meaning of earlier episodes) as deliberate narrative strategy; connect this to Barthes's mechanism of enigma and to deferred interpretation in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer point / intermediary subject (dispatching narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of a strategically dominant temporal position (a 'transfer point') in the narrative from which many analepses/prolepses are launched and to which they return (e.g., Proust's position 5 'insomnias' functioning as an 'intermediary subject').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map which narrative moment(s) act as hubs controlling recollections; these positions function as anchors that make possible the zigzag movement of memory-created instances and can be essential to the macrostructure of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis / acceleration vs anachrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate simple ellipsis (a leap forward without return—an acceleration in narrative time) from anachrony: ellipsis is not an anachrony because it does not produce a temporal displacement that is then returned to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark transitions that skip intervening time but do not create out-of-order retro- or proleptic narratives with a hyphen (successive) rather than a bracket (anachrony). Treat ellipsis as part of duration/speed analysis rather than order.
